course.title: Go Programming for Networked Services
course.subtitle: Build Go programs and HTTP services with clear types, explicit errors and safe concurrency.
course.description: A practical Go course covering the toolchain, packages, types, functions, slices, maps, structs, interfaces, error handling, goroutines, channels, contexts, HTTP handlers, testing, service security and delivery. Learners build a small network service and practise cancellation, diagnostics and predictable API contracts.
target_audience: Learners interested in backend, cloud or networked services
Programmers moving from a first language to concurrent systems
prerequisites: Familiarity with variables, functions and data structures
outcomes: Create and build a Go module
Use Go types, functions and package visibility
Choose slices, maps and structs for appropriate data
Explain interfaces and explicit error handling
Coordinate goroutines using channels and context
Build HTTP handlers with documented contracts
Write table-driven tests and inspect concurrent behaviour
Deliver a configurable Go service with basic security controls
equipment: Terminal and local HTTP testing client
course.accessibility: Code examples are selectable text; concurrency diagrams must be described in text. Exercises include expected results and do not rely on colour alone.

sections.title: Go Fundamentals and Program Structure
sections.description: Understand Go tooling, packages, types and basic control flow.

lessons.title: Go toolchain and project workflow
lessons.body_markdown:
## Go toolchain and project workflow

Go includes a compiler, formatter, test runner and other tools in its toolchain. A module defines a project's module path and dependencies in `go.mod`. `go run` can build and execute a package during development, while `go build` produces a binary for deployment. `gofmt` formats source consistently; formatting is not proof of correctness. A reproducible project documents its Go version and commands and keeps dependency changes visible in version control.

### Worked example

Create a module, add a `main` package, run it, build it and format the source with `gofmt`.

### Common failure to avoid

Do not assume code that runs through a local editor has a reproducible module configuration.

### Check your understanding

Explain the data flow and lifecycle in your own words. Identify the caller, the resource or value being managed, the expected success result and the failure or cancellation path. A network service must continue to behave correctly when requests are malformed, slow or disconnected.
lessons.exercise: Write the setup and build commands another learner would use from a clean checkout.
key_takeaways: Explain the purpose and behaviour of go toolchain and project workflow.
Identify one concurrency, error-handling or API contract that affects the design.

lessons.title: Packages, declarations and visibility
lessons.body_markdown:
## Packages, declarations and visibility

Go code is organised into packages. A package name describes the files' package, while an import path identifies the package to other code. An identifier beginning with an uppercase letter is exported; a lowercase identifier is unexported outside its package. Keep package responsibilities focused and avoid circular imports. A `main` package with a `main` function forms an executable entry point. Package boundaries should express ownership of concepts rather than merely mirror the number of files.

### Worked example

Create `student` and `report` packages, exporting only the types and functions that another package needs.

### Common failure to avoid

Do not export every field or helper automatically; an unnecessarily broad API is harder to change safely.

### Check your understanding

Explain the data flow and lifecycle in your own words. Identify the caller, the resource or value being managed, the expected success result and the failure or cancellation path. A network service must continue to behave correctly when requests are malformed, slow or disconnected.
lessons.exercise: Draw the import direction among packages in a small course-report application.
key_takeaways: Explain the purpose and behaviour of packages, declarations and visibility.
Identify one concurrency, error-handling or API contract that affects the design.

lessons.title: Types, zero values and control flow
lessons.body_markdown:
## Types, zero values and control flow

Go is statically typed and uses explicit declarations or short variable declarations with `:=`. Its zero values are defined for each type, but a zero value is not necessarily valid domain data. `if`, `for` and `switch` form the main control-flow tools; Go has no separate `while` keyword. Conditions must be Boolean, and `for range` iterates across arrays, slices, maps, strings and channels with type-specific behaviour. Use clear names and validate external values even when a variable has a safe zero value.

### Worked example

Write a loop that totals scores and uses a condition to count passing results.

### Common failure to avoid

Do not interpret a zero value as proof that a required input was provided.

### Check your understanding

Explain the data flow and lifecycle in your own words. Identify the caller, the resource or value being managed, the expected success result and the failure or cancellation path. A network service must continue to behave correctly when requests are malformed, slow or disconnected.
lessons.exercise: Explain the zero values of an integer, Boolean, string, slice and map and how each affects a domain model.
key_takeaways: Explain the purpose and behaviour of types, zero values and control flow.
Identify one concurrency, error-handling or API contract that affects the design.

lessons.title: Functions, multiple results and pointers
lessons.body_markdown:
## Functions, multiple results and pointers

Go functions can return multiple values, commonly a result and an error. Parameters are passed by value; pointers allow a function to access the same underlying object or update caller-owned state. Use a pointer because the contract requires shared mutation or avoids a meaningful copy, not simply because a value is a struct. Avoid returning pointers to data with an invalid lifetime and handle nil pointers deliberately. A clear function contract documents what each result means.

### Worked example

Write a parser that returns `(int, error)` for a score and test valid, malformed and out-of-range input.

### Common failure to avoid

Do not ignore an error result with `_` unless the failure is genuinely irrelevant and that decision is safe.

### Check your understanding

Explain the data flow and lifecycle in your own words. Identify the caller, the resource or value being managed, the expected success result and the failure or cancellation path. A network service must continue to behave correctly when requests are malformed, slow or disconnected.
lessons.exercise: Design a function signature for loading a student record and explain its result and error values.
key_takeaways: Explain the purpose and behaviour of functions, multiple results and pointers.
Identify one concurrency, error-handling or API contract that affects the design.

sections.description: Use slices, maps, structs, methods and explicit errors.

lessons.title: Slices, arrays and capacity
lessons.body_markdown:
## Slices, arrays and capacity

An array has a fixed length that is part of its type. A slice is a descriptor over an underlying array, containing a pointer, length and capacity. Multiple slices may share the same underlying storage, so changing an element through one slice can be visible through another. Appending may allocate a new backing array when capacity is exceeded, which changes sharing behaviour. Use `make` when choosing initial length or capacity and do not confuse `len` with `cap`.

### Worked example

Create two slices from the same array, update an element and append enough values to observe possible reallocation.

### Common failure to avoid

Do not assume a slice is an independent copy of the elements it references.

### Check your understanding

Explain the data flow and lifecycle in your own words. Identify the caller, the resource or value being managed, the expected success result and the failure or cancellation path. A network service must continue to behave correctly when requests are malformed, slow or disconnected.
lessons.exercise: Draw the relationship between an array, a slice's length and capacity, and its backing storage.
key_takeaways: Explain the purpose and behaviour of slices, arrays and capacity.

lessons.title: Maps and data modelling
lessons.body_markdown:
## Maps and data modelling

A map associates keys with values and supports lookup, insertion and deletion. A lookup can return a second Boolean that indicates whether the key existed, which is different from the zero value of the mapped type. A nil map can be read but cannot accept new entries; initialise it with `make` or a literal before writing. Map iteration order is not guaranteed, so sort keys when stable display order matters. Choose keys that have stable equality semantics and document uniqueness requirements.

### Worked example

Use a map keyed by matriculation number and distinguish a missing student from an existing student whose count is zero.

### Common failure to avoid

Do not depend on map iteration order or write to a nil map.

### Check your understanding

Explain the data flow and lifecycle in your own words. Identify the caller, the resource or value being managed, the expected success result and the failure or cancellation path. A network service must continue to behave correctly when requests are malformed, slow or disconnected.
lessons.exercise: Create a student lookup map and produce a deterministic sorted report.
key_takeaways: Explain the purpose and behaviour of maps and data modelling.
Identify one concurrency, error-handling or API contract that affects the design.

lessons.title: Structs, methods and interfaces
lessons.body_markdown:
## Structs, methods and interfaces

A struct groups related fields. Methods attach behaviour to a type using receiver parameters; pointer receivers can mutate the original value or avoid copying larger structs. Interfaces in Go are satisfied implicitly when a type implements the required method set. Small interfaces make dependencies easier to test, while large interfaces create unnecessary coupling. A nil interface and an interface containing a typed nil value are not always equivalent, which is an important edge case in API design.

### Worked example

Define a `Student` struct with a method that computes a grade and an interface for exporting a report.

### Common failure to avoid

Do not create broad interfaces before identifying which behaviour a consumer actually needs.

### Check your understanding

Explain the data flow and lifecycle in your own words. Identify the caller, the resource or value being managed, the expected success result and the failure or cancellation path. A network service must continue to behave correctly when requests are malformed, slow or disconnected.
lessons.exercise: Implement one report exporter and show how a second implementation could satisfy the same interface.
key_takeaways: Explain the purpose and behaviour of structs, methods and interfaces.
Identify one concurrency, error-handling or API contract that affects the design.

lessons.title: Errors, wrapping and validation
lessons.body_markdown:
## Errors, wrapping and validation

Go commonly represents expected failures with the `error` interface. Callers should check returned errors and decide whether to return, wrap, translate or handle them. Error wrapping with `%w` preserves the underlying cause for inspection. Avoid using panic for ordinary invalid user input; panic is for conditions where normal recovery is not appropriate or a programmer invariant is broken. Validate data at boundaries and include enough context to diagnose which operation failed.

### Worked example

Write a function that loads a record and wraps a lower-level read error with the record identifier.

### Common failure to avoid

Do not discard returned errors or panic on a routine malformed form value.

### Check your understanding

Explain the data flow and lifecycle in your own words. Identify the caller, the resource or value being managed, the expected success result and the failure or cancellation path. A network service must continue to behave correctly when requests are malformed, slow or disconnected.
lessons.exercise: Create an error-handling policy for not-found, invalid-input and storage-failure conditions.
key_takeaways: Explain the purpose and behaviour of errors, wrapping and validation.
Identify one concurrency, error-handling or API contract that affects the design.

sections.title: Concurrency and Networked Services
sections.description: Understand goroutines, channels, contexts and HTTP handlers.

lessons.title: Goroutines and concurrent execution
lessons.body_markdown:
## Goroutines and concurrent execution

A goroutine is a function executing concurrently with other goroutines. Starting one is lightweight, but concurrent execution introduces coordination and shared-state risks. A program must define how workers finish and how errors are reported. A goroutine that is started and never joined or otherwise observed can leak work and hide failures. Concurrency should solve a real coordination or throughput problem, not serve as decoration. Use the race detector during testing when possible.

### Worked example

Start independent calculations as goroutines and wait for all of them to finish before printing the combined result.

### Common failure to avoid

Do not return from `main` while required goroutines are still doing work.

### Check your understanding

Explain the data flow and lifecycle in your own words. Identify the caller, the resource or value being managed, the expected success result and the failure or cancellation path. A network service must continue to behave correctly when requests are malformed, slow or disconnected.
lessons.exercise: Draw a lifecycle showing who starts a worker, who waits and how worker errors are observed.
key_takeaways: Explain the purpose and behaviour of goroutines and concurrent execution.
Identify one concurrency, error-handling or API contract that affects the design.

lessons.title: Channels and synchronization
lessons.body_markdown:
## Channels and synchronization

Channels communicate values between goroutines and can coordinate work. An unbuffered channel synchronises sender and receiver; a buffered channel can hold a limited number of values before send blocks. The sender and receiver must agree on who closes a channel. Sending on a closed channel panics, and receiving from a closed channel returns zero values after queued data is exhausted. A `select` statement handles multiple channel operations and can include a cancellation case.

### Worked example

Build a worker pool that receives jobs from a channel and sends results back to a collector.

### Common failure to avoid

Do not close a channel from a receiver that does not own the sending lifecycle.

### Check your understanding

Explain the data flow and lifecycle in your own words. Identify the caller, the resource or value being managed, the expected success result and the failure or cancellation path. A network service must continue to behave correctly when requests are malformed, slow or disconnected.
lessons.exercise: Explain how the worker pool terminates and how it avoids leaving blocked goroutines behind.
key_takeaways: Explain the purpose and behaviour of channels and synchronization.
Identify one concurrency, error-handling or API contract that affects the design.

lessons.title: Context, cancellation and timeouts
lessons.body_markdown:
## Context, cancellation and timeouts

The `context` package carries cancellation signals, deadlines and request-scoped values across API boundaries. A caller should pass a context to operations that may block or outlive the caller's interest. Functions should respect `ctx.Done()` and stop work promptly when cancellation is requested. Context values are not a general-purpose parameter bag; use them only for request-scoped data crossing API boundaries. A server handler's request context is cancelled when the request is cancelled or the handler finishes.

### Worked example

Add a timeout to a simulated network request and ensure the worker stops when the context is cancelled.

### Common failure to avoid

Do not create background work that ignores cancellation after the user has abandoned the request.

### Check your understanding

Explain the data flow and lifecycle in your own words. Identify the caller, the resource or value being managed, the expected success result and the failure or cancellation path. A network service must continue to behave correctly when requests are malformed, slow or disconnected.
lessons.exercise: Trace a request from handler to service to storage and identify where context must be passed.
key_takeaways: Explain the purpose and behaviour of context, cancellation and timeouts.
Identify one concurrency, error-handling or API contract that affects the design.

lessons.title: HTTP handlers and API contracts
lessons.body_markdown:
## HTTP handlers and API contracts

Go's standard HTTP packages provide primitives for building servers and handlers. A handler receives a request and writes a response. Validate the method, path parameters and body before applying a state change. Use the correct content type and status code, and encode JSON through a JSON encoder rather than string concatenation. A handler should delegate business rules to a service and map domain outcomes to HTTP responses. Do not treat a route's obscurity as access control.

### Worked example

Write a handler that returns a JSON list of courses and a clear error response for an unsupported method.

### Common failure to avoid

Do not write part of a success response before discovering that the request is invalid.

### Check your understanding

Explain the data flow and lifecycle in your own words. Identify the caller, the resource or value being managed, the expected success result and the failure or cancellation path. A network service must continue to behave correctly when requests are malformed, slow or disconnected.
lessons.exercise: Document request and response shapes for a course-list endpoint and an enrolment endpoint.
key_takeaways: Explain the purpose and behaviour of http handlers and api contracts.
Identify one concurrency, error-handling or API contract that affects the design.

lessons.title: Unit and table-driven testing
lessons.body_markdown:
## Unit and table-driven testing

Go's `testing` package supports test functions and benchmarks. Table-driven tests make it easy to cover related cases with named inputs and expected results. Tests should not depend on map iteration order, current time or external services unless those dependencies are controlled. Use test helpers when they improve clarity, and do not hide useful failure context. Run the race detector for concurrent code where supported. A test should be repeatable and fail clearly when behaviour changes.

### Worked example

Write table-driven tests for a score parser covering valid, empty, malformed, boundary and out-of-range values.

### Common failure to avoid

Do not write tests that pass only because they depend on a particular iteration order.

### Check your understanding

Explain the data flow and lifecycle in your own words. Identify the caller, the resource or value being managed, the expected success result and the failure or cancellation path. A network service must continue to behave correctly when requests are malformed, slow or disconnected.
lessons.exercise: Create a test table with named cases, inputs and expected errors or results.
key_takeaways: Explain the purpose and behaviour of unit and table-driven testing.

lessons.title: Debugging, profiling and observability
lessons.body_markdown:
## Debugging, profiling and observability

A debugger can inspect goroutines, stack traces and variable state. Logs should provide context such as operation and request identifiers without recording passwords, tokens or private payloads. Profiling helps identify CPU, memory or blocking bottlenecks under representative load. Optimisation should be driven by measurement rather than guessing. For concurrent programs, a race detector can reveal unsynchronised access that ordinary tests might not consistently reproduce.

### Worked example

Reproduce a shared-map race in a controlled exercise, run the race detector and protect the shared state correctly.

### Common failure to avoid

Do not assume one passing run proves a concurrent program is race-free.

### Check your understanding

Explain the data flow and lifecycle in your own words. Identify the caller, the resource or value being managed, the expected success result and the failure or cancellation path. A network service must continue to behave correctly when requests are malformed, slow or disconnected.
lessons.exercise: Write a short incident note with reproduction, evidence, root cause, correction and regression test.
key_takeaways: Explain the purpose and behaviour of debugging, profiling and observability.

lessons.title: API security and reliability controls
lessons.body_markdown:
## API security and reliability controls

A network service must treat requests as untrusted. Apply authentication and authorisation before returning protected data or changing state. Validate request sizes and field constraints, use parameterised storage operations and avoid returning internal stack traces. Rate limits and timeouts help reduce resource exhaustion; CORS controls browser cross-origin access but is not an authentication mechanism. Secrets belong in deployment configuration, not source code. Security controls must be enforced server-side, even when the normal user interface hides an action.

### Worked example

Create a threat checklist for an enrolment endpoint covering identity, permissions, input size, request rate and error responses.

### Common failure to avoid

Do not mistake CORS or an obscure route name for access control.

### Check your understanding

Explain the data flow and lifecycle in your own words. Identify the caller, the resource or value being managed, the expected success result and the failure or cancellation path. A network service must continue to behave correctly when requests are malformed, slow or disconnected.
lessons.exercise: Write a security test for a learner attempting to access another learner's enrolment.
key_takeaways: Explain the purpose and behaviour of api security and reliability controls.
Identify one concurrency, error-handling or API contract that affects the design.

lessons.title: Build, configure and release a Go service
lessons.body_markdown:
## Build, configure and release a Go service

A deployable Go service needs repeatable builds, explicit configuration and graceful shutdown. Configuration can come from environment variables or a structured file, but required values should be validated at startup. Do not hard-code credentials. Handle server shutdown so active requests can finish and resources can close. The README should explain build, test, run, configuration and known limitations. Delivery evidence includes a clean build and tests, not only a process that happened to run locally.

### Worked example

Build an HTTP service with a health route, environment-based port configuration and graceful shutdown.

### Common failure to avoid

Do not swallow startup errors or terminate active requests abruptly without a shutdown policy.

### Check your understanding

Explain the data flow and lifecycle in your own words. Identify the caller, the resource or value being managed, the expected success result and the failure or cancellation path. A network service must continue to behave correctly when requests are malformed, slow or disconnected.
lessons.exercise: Submit a service with endpoint documentation, tests, configuration notes and reproducible run instructions.
key_takeaways: Explain the purpose and behaviour of build, configure and release a go service.

assessment.title: Go Programming for Networked Services Final Assessment
assessment.instructions: Answer all questions and show reasoning for concurrency and error handling. Code must build with the stated toolchain and include tests.

questions.prompt: Explain how a Go slice relates to its backing array and why two slices may observe the same element mutation.
Write a Go function that parses a score and returns a value with an error for malformed or out-of-range input.
Design a worker pool using jobs and result channels. Explain how workers terminate and how the caller collects all results.
Specify an HTTP endpoint for course enrolment, including method, body, status codes and failure behaviour.
Create table-driven tests for a function with normal, boundary, malformed and cancellation cases.
Submit the Course Enrolment HTTP Service with configuration, tests and endpoint documentation.

final_project.title: Course Enrolment HTTP Service
final_project.brief: Build a Go HTTP service that lists courses and accepts enrolment requests in a controlled local environment. Validate request bodies, return consistent JSON, keep domain rules outside handlers and use context for request-scoped work. Add tests for success, bad requests, not-found conditions and cancellation where relevant.
deliverables: At least 10 tests with expected results
README with configuration and run instructions
Short design note about concurrency and cancellation
acceptance_criteria: Routes return the documented status and JSON response shape
Domain rules are testable outside the handler
Tests cover normal, boundary and error cases
Configuration is external to source code
Service starts and shuts down predictably
Protected operations verify identity and permission server-side
